questions.question: An IS auditor led the engineering of a company's IAM system and joined the audit function six months ago. The auditor is now assigned to audit that system. What is the MOST appropriate action?

options.A: Proceed, since six months have passed since the transfer
options.B: Proceed, with an independent peer review of the audit conclusions
options.C: Reassign the engagement to an auditor with no involvement
options.D: Proceed, with the project team validating the findings

questions.key_concept: Auditing a system you designed or built is a self-review threat; removing the threat by reassignment beats mitigating it.
questions.pre_read: Notice the auditor's former role on the same system. Decide whether the threat should be mitigated or removed.
questions.correct_explanation: Leading the build of the IAM system and then auditing it is a classic self-review threat: the auditor would be judging their own design decisions. Reassigning the engagement to someone with no involvement removes the threat entirely. A peer review of conclusions is a reasonable safeguard, but the fieldwork, sampling and judgments would still come from the conflicted auditor, so the threat remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Six months does not cure self-review. The auditor would still be assessing design decisions they made personally.
wrong_explanations.B: Peer review mitigates the threat but leaves the conflicted auditor doing the fieldwork and judgments; removing the threat is stronger.
wrong_explanations.D: Letting the auditee validate findings adds a second independence problem rather than solving the first.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes time cures self-review, and D hands the auditee control over the findings.
Final two: C beats B because reassignment removes the self-review threat, while peer review only mitigates it after the work is done.
Exam cue: auditing your own recent design work is a severe self-review threat, so reassign; low, unrelated threats are disclosed and safeguarded instead.

questions.question: An IS auditor is testing whether an application enforces password complexity rules. Which of the following provides the MOST reliable evidence that the control is operating effectively in production?

options.A: A signed statement from the IT manager confirming the setting
options.B: Auditor inspection of the system's password parameter settings
options.C: A vendor document stating the product supports complexity rules
options.D: Auditor's own noncompliant password attempt on a test account

questions.key_concept: Evidence the auditor obtains directly by observation or reperformance is more reliable than representations, documents or configuration inspection.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem asks whether the control is operating, not merely configured. Rank options by who generated the evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: Evidence the auditor obtains directly by observing or reperforming a control is the most reliable, because it does not depend on anyone else's claim. Attempting a noncompliant password and watching the system reject it proves the rule operates in production now. Inspecting parameters is strong evidence of design, but settings can be overridden by exceptions or other policies.

wrong_explanations.A: A management representation is the weakest evidence type. It is a useful starting point, never proof that a control operates.
wrong_explanations.B: Inspecting settings shows the control is configured, not that it works; exceptions or overrides could still let weak passwords through.
wrong_explanations.C: A vendor document describes product capability in general, not how this installation is configured or whether the rule is enabled.

tips: Eliminate: A is a management representation and C describes product capability, not this system's configuration.
Final two: D beats B because reperformance proves the control operates, while inspecting settings only proves it is configured.
Exam cue: for MOST reliable evidence, prefer what the auditor directly observes or reperforms over anything someone hands over.

questions.question: An IS auditor wants to confirm that a workflow enforces second-person approval on production schedule changes. Which testing approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Substantive testing of schedule values against production output
options.B: Compliance testing of sampled changes for approval evidence
options.C: Interviews with planners about following the approval workflow
options.D: Inspection of the workflow's approval configuration settings

questions.key_concept: Compliance (control) testing shows whether a control operated over a period; substantive testing checks the accuracy of the data itself.
questions.pre_read: Notice the objective is about a control being enforced, not about data accuracy. Then ask which evidence shows it operated over time.
questions.correct_explanation: The objective is whether a control, second-person approval, is operating, so compliance testing fits. Sampling actual changes and checking each for evidence of approval shows the control operated across the period. Inspecting the configuration is useful evidence of design, but settings show only how the workflow is set up today, not whether changes were approved throughout the period.

wrong_explanations.A: Substantive testing checks whether the schedule data is correct. It does not show whether the approval control operated.
wrong_explanations.C: Inquiry alone is weak evidence. Planners describing the workflow does not prove each change was actually approved.
wrong_explanations.D: Configuration inspection shows design at one point in time, not that approvals happened on changes across the period.

tips: Eliminate: A tests data accuracy rather than the control, and C relies on inquiry, which never stands alone.
Final two: B beats D because sampling actual changes proves the control operated over time; settings show only its design today.
Exam cue: when the objective is whether a control works, choose compliance testing of a sample over design inspection.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds cardholder data stored unencrypted in a development database for over a year. To whom is it MOST appropriate to address the formal audit report?

options.A: The development manager who owns the affected database
options.B: The card brands and the company's acquiring bank
options.C: The audit committee, with copies to accountable executives
options.D: The CISO, as owner of the security program

questions.key_concept: Formal audit reports go to the governance body the audit function reports to, with copies to management accountable for remediation.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word formal. Ask which audience the audit function reports to, rather than who will fix the issue.
questions.correct_explanation: Formal audit reports are addressed to the audit committee or equivalent governance body, which oversees the audit function and holds management to account. Executives responsible for the affected systems receive copies so they can commit to remediation. The CISO is an important stakeholder and will likely act on the finding, but is part of management being reported on, not the reporting line.

wrong_explanations.A: The development manager is too low to own remediation of a year-long cardholder data exposure, and is part of the auditee.
wrong_explanations.B: External notification decisions belong to management and legal counsel. The auditor reports internally through the governance line.
wrong_explanations.D: The CISO is a key operational stakeholder, but formal reports go to the governance body overseeing audit, not one manager.

tips: Eliminate: A reports too low within the auditee, and B makes the auditor notify outsiders, which is management's decision.
Final two: C beats D because the formal report goes to the audit committee; the CISO is management, not the reporting line.
Exam cue: formal audit report addressee questions point to the audit committee or board, with accountable management copied.

questions.question: A CIO calls a 24/7 anomaly-detection tool a 'continuous auditing' capability; its alerts go to IT operations for response. What is the IS auditor's MOST appropriate observation?

options.A: The label fits, as detection runs automatically around the clock
options.B: The tool needs audit committee approval before it continues
options.C: It is continuous monitoring, since operations owns the response
options.D: It becomes continuous auditing once auditors can read alerts

questions.key_concept: Continuous monitoring is management's operational control; continuous auditing is performed by the audit function for independent assurance.
questions.pre_read: Notice who receives and acts on the alerts. Classify the capability by owner and purpose, not by technology.
questions.correct_explanation: The difference between continuous auditing and continuous monitoring is ownership and purpose, not technology. A tool whose alerts are handled by IT operations is a management control, which is continuous monitoring. Giving auditors read access does not change that; continuous auditing is designed and run by the audit function to provide independent assurance, although auditors may assess and rely on management's monitoring.

wrong_explanations.A: Running automatically around the clock describes the technique, not the owner. Both monitoring and auditing can run continuously.
wrong_explanations.B: Operational tools are management's decision. The audit committee oversees audit, not approval of management's monitoring tools.
wrong_explanations.D: Read access lets auditors use the output, but operations still owns the tool and response, so it remains monitoring.

tips: Eliminate: A labels the tool by its round-the-clock automation, which monitoring and auditing tools share, and B misplaces approval of operational tools with the audit committee.
Final two: C beats D because ownership defines the capability; read access does not turn management's monitoring into audit work.
Exam cue: who owns and acts on it decides the label; management runs monitoring, the audit function runs auditing.

questions.question: An IS auditor tests 60 of 6,800 privileged-access transactions and finds 6 failures (10%) against a 5% tolerable rate. What is the auditor's MOST appropriate next step?

options.A: Pass the control if the six failures share one cause
options.B: Conclude the control is not operating effectively
options.C: Expand the sample to refine the deviation-rate estimate before concluding
options.D: Replace the six failed items with six new selections

questions.key_concept: When the sample deviation rate clearly exceeds the tolerable rate, the auditor cannot rely on the control and evaluates the deviations' cause.
questions.pre_read: Compare the sample rate with the tolerable rate. Ask whether more testing could realistically change the conclusion.
questions.correct_explanation: A 10% sample deviation rate against a 5% tolerable rate means the auditor cannot rely on the control, whatever allowance is made for sampling risk. The auditor concludes it is not operating effectively, evaluates the cause and nature of the deviations, and adjusts substantive work. Extending suits results near the threshold; even a far larger sample would almost certainly leave the upper deviation limit above 5%.

wrong_explanations.A: Shared causes make failures look like one problem, which tempts candidates to discount them. Each deviation counts against the tolerable rate; the cause guides remediation, not the conclusion.
wrong_explanations.C: Extension helps when results are borderline. With 10% against 5%, more items would only delay an inevitable conclusion.
wrong_explanations.D: Swapping failed items seems to give a cleaner sample, but deviations found must be evaluated, not replaced. Replacing them hides a 10% rate already above the tolerable rate.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because A excuses failures that share a cause, and D swaps failed items for new ones; every deviation found counts against the tolerable rate.
Final two: B beats C because extending a sample helps only near the threshold; 10% against 5% is already conclusive.
Exam cue: if the sample rate already exceeds the tolerable rate by a wide margin, conclude rather than keep sampling.

questions.question: An IS auditor reduced independent testing because business-unit control self-assessments rate controls as effective, yet security incidents keep occurring. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Self-assessment is replacing, not supplementing, audit testing
options.B: Self-assessors lack sufficient technical expertise in IS controls
options.C: The incident response process is failing to contain new incidents
options.D: Self-assessments should be run by the audit function instead

questions.key_concept: Control self-assessment complements but never replaces independent audit assurance, especially when self-reports conflict with actual outcomes.
questions.pre_read: Notice two facts: the auditor reduced testing, and results contradict incidents. Look for the root cause, not a symptom.
questions.correct_explanation: Control self-assessment complements independent audit work; it cannot replace it. Here self-reported results contradict actual incidents, yet the audit function has stepped back, so no one is providing reliable assurance. That structural over-reliance is the root concern. Weak assessor expertise is a real contributing cause, but even expert self-assessors would not justify replacing independent testing.

wrong_explanations.B: Limited expertise contributes to unreliable results, but it is a cause, not the core problem of reduced independent assurance.
wrong_explanations.C: Recurring incidents point toward incident response, but the stem gives no facts on containment. The auditor's concern is that unvalidated self-ratings replaced independent testing.
wrong_explanations.D: In CSA, process owners assess their own controls and audit facilitates or reviews; moving the assessment to audit misreads CSA and leaves testing reduced.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because C blames incident handling, which the facts do not implicate, and D moves CSA to audit, though in CSA process owners assess their own controls.
Final two: A beats B because over-reliance on self-assessment is the root cause; assessor skill is only one contributing factor.
Exam cue: control self-assessment supplements independent assurance and never replaces it; look for the option naming that over-reliance.

questions.subtopic: Effect of Laws and Regulations on Audit Planning
questions.question: A cross-border data-transfer law takes effect in six months and will affect a logistics company's daily shipping data flows. What is the IS auditor's BEST action for the upcoming audit plan?

options.A: Wait until the law is in force, then test compliance
options.B: Interpret the law independently and add tailored tests
options.C: Confirm its impact with legal and compliance, then adjust scope
options.D: Recommend that external counsel own the compliance response

questions.key_concept: The IS auditor must understand regulatory impact for planning, but relies on legal and compliance for interpretation rather than reading the law alone.
questions.pre_read: Notice the law is not yet in force. Ask who should interpret it and when the audit plan should respond.
questions.correct_explanation: The auditor must consider laws and regulations that affect the audit subject when planning, and six months gives time to build them into scope. Legal interpretation, however, belongs to legal and compliance. Interpreting the law alone risks testing against a misreading and puts the auditor in a role they are not qualified for, so coordinating first and then adjusting scope is better.

wrong_explanations.A: Waiting forfeits the chance to assess readiness and leaves the plan reacting to non-compliance after the fact.
wrong_explanations.B: The auditor needs to understand the law, but solo interpretation risks a misreading; legal and compliance own interpretation.
wrong_explanations.D: Compliance remains management's responsibility. The auditor's task here is to adjust the audit plan, not to assign ownership.

tips: Eliminate: A waits until noncompliance can occur instead of planning for a known change, and D reassigns compliance ownership rather than adjusting the audit plan.
Final two: C beats B because legal and compliance own interpretation; the auditor translates their view into audit scope.
Exam cue: for new regulations, the auditor coordinates with legal and compliance, then reflects the impact in the risk-based plan.

questions.question: A credit-scoring model is retrained every month, and engineering releases changes every week. The audit committee wants earlier assurance. Which approach is MOST appropriate for the IS audit team?

options.A: Defer the audit until the model stops changing monthly
options.B: Outsource the engagement to an external audit firm
options.C: An agile audit delivering assurance in short sprints
options.D: A traditional audit cycle with an interim progress update

questions.key_concept: Agile auditing suits fast-changing subjects, agile organizations and stakeholders who want frequent, incremental assurance.
questions.pre_read: Notice three facts: monthly change, weekly releases and a request for earlier assurance. Match the audit cadence to them.
questions.correct_explanation: All three facts favor agile auditing: the subject changes monthly, engineering works in short cycles, and the committee wants earlier assurance. Short sprints with incremental reporting keep conclusions current. A traditional cycle with an interim update offers some earlier visibility, but the main conclusions would still arrive months later, after several retrains, describing a model that no longer exists.

wrong_explanations.A: A continuously retrained model may never stabilize, and deferring leaves the committee without the assurance it requested.
wrong_explanations.B: Outsourcing changes who audits, not the cadence; a traditional cycle run by any firm would still deliver stale conclusions.
wrong_explanations.D: Interim updates are a common reporting practice, but a progress report is not an opinion, and assurance must move at the pace of its subject.

tips: Eliminate: A waits for stability that may never come, and B changes the auditor without changing the cadence.
Final two: C beats D because sprints keep pace with monthly change; an interim update still leaves conclusions stale.
Exam cue: fast-changing subject plus requests for earlier assurance point to agile auditing over a traditional cycle.

questions.question: An audit function's quality assurance (QA) program relies on annual self-assessments by team leads; its last external review was 12 years ago. What is the GREATEST weakness for the IS audit lead to report?

options.A: Reviews cover documentation but not fieldwork techniques
options.B: The program has not been redesigned in over a decade
options.C: Self-assessments raise few findings each year
options.D: No independent review has validated the QA program

questions.key_concept: A QA program needs periodic independent external assessment; self-assessment alone gives the audit committee unverified, potentially false assurance.
questions.pre_read: Notice who performs the reviews and when outsiders last looked. Ask which gap lets every other weakness go unnoticed.
questions.correct_explanation: A quality assurance program needs both internal assessment and periodic independent external review, commonly at least every five years. With only self-assessment by the people being assessed and no outside review for 12 years, the committee's assurance rests on self-attestation. Narrow review scope is a real gap, but without independent challenge no one objective is positioned to detect it or any other weakness.

wrong_explanations.A: Narrow scope matters, but an independent reviewer would identify it; the lack of independence is the deeper, enabling weakness.
wrong_explanations.B: Age alone is not a weakness. A long-running program can remain effective if it is independently validated.
wrong_explanations.C: Few findings may reflect good performance or weak self-review; it is a symptom to investigate, not the weakness itself.

tips: Eliminate: B treats age as a defect, and C reads a low finding count as a weakness in itself.
Final two: D beats A because missing independent review lets every gap, including scope, go undetected.
Exam cue: for QA programs, independence of review outranks scope or format; self-assessment alone gives false assurance.

questions.subtopic: Using the Work of Other Experts
questions.question: An IS auditor without cryptographic expertise engages an external cryptographer to assess an encryption design. What should the auditor do FIRST before relying on the cryptographer's conclusions?

options.A: Obtain a signed confidentiality agreement from the cryptographer
options.B: Evaluate the cryptographer's competence and objectivity
options.C: Reperform a sample of the cryptographer's tests
options.D: Have the cryptographer report directly to the audit committee

questions.key_concept: Before relying on an expert, the IS auditor assesses competence, objectivity and relevance of the work, and keeps responsibility for conclusions.
questions.pre_read: Notice the auditor lacks the expertise. Ask what makes someone else's work safe to rely on.
questions.correct_explanation: Before relying on an expert's work, the IS auditor must assess the expert's competence, objectivity and the relevance of the work, because the auditor keeps responsibility for the conclusion. Reperforming tests can add assurance, but an auditor without cryptographic skill cannot reperform them meaningfully, and reperformance does not show the expert was qualified or independent.

wrong_explanations.A: A confidentiality agreement protects the client's information. It is a contractual matter and says nothing about whether the expert's conclusions can be relied on.
wrong_explanations.C: Reperforming an expert's tests is a recognized evaluation step, though it follows vetting the expert: reliance starts with who did the work.
wrong_explanations.D: The IS auditor remains responsible for the audit conclusion, so the expert's work must flow through the auditor, not around them.

tips: Eliminate: A protects the client's data, which says nothing about whether the work can be relied on, and D bypasses the auditor, who stays responsible for the conclusion.
Final two: B beats C because reliance rests first on the expert's qualifications and independence, which reperforming tests cannot replace.
Exam cue: before using another expert's work, assess their competence and objectivity first.

questions.subtopic: Types of IS Audit Reports / Opinion Types
questions.question: An IS auditor finds two significant control weaknesses, but other major control areas operate effectively and there was no scope limitation. Which opinion is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Unmodified opinion, as most controls operate effectively
options.B: Qualified opinion, except for the noted weaknesses
options.C: Adverse opinion, given the significant weaknesses found
options.D: Disclaimer of opinion, owing to insufficient evidence

questions.key_concept: Opinion type turns on significance and pervasiveness: qualified for contained significant issues, adverse for pervasive ones, disclaimer for scope limits.
questions.pre_read: Ask two questions: are the issues significant, and are they pervasive? Then check for any scope limitation.
questions.correct_explanation: A qualified opinion fits when specific issues are significant but not pervasive: controls are effective except for the named weaknesses. Here the problems are confined to two areas while other major areas work. An adverse opinion is reserved for weaknesses so pervasive that controls are ineffective overall, which would overstate two contained findings and mislead readers.

wrong_explanations.A: An unmodified opinion signals no significant issues. Two significant weaknesses must be reflected in the opinion, not left out of it.
wrong_explanations.C: Adverse opinions apply when weaknesses are pervasive across the area. Effective controls elsewhere show these weaknesses are contained.
wrong_explanations.D: A disclaimer is used when the auditor cannot obtain enough evidence, such as under a scope limitation. None occurred here.

tips: Eliminate: A gives a clean opinion despite two significant weaknesses, and D requires a scope limitation the stem rules out.
Final two: B beats C because the weaknesses are significant but contained, not pervasive across the control environment.
Exam cue: significant but contained points to qualified; pervasive points to adverse; missing evidence points to disclaimer.

questions.question: An IS auditor is ranking four risks for next year's risk-based audit plan. Which risk should the auditor rank FIRST?

options.A: A risk with medium likelihood, medium impact and easily quantified loss
options.B: A risk with low likelihood, high impact and a tested failover
options.C: A risk with high likelihood, high impact and regulatory exposure
options.D: A risk with low likelihood but very high reputational impact

questions.key_concept: Risk-based audit planning ranks risks on combined likelihood and impact, adjusted for existing mitigation, not on a single dimension.
questions.pre_read: Score each option on both likelihood and impact before reacting to dramatic wording.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk-based prioritization weighs likelihood and impact together. The risk with high likelihood and high impact, compounded by regulatory exposure, scores highest on the combined rating. The reputational risk has an even larger impact, but its low likelihood pulls its combined rating well below, so ranking on worst-case impact alone would misdirect limited audit resources.

wrong_explanations.A: Medium on both dimensions gives a moderate score. Being easy to quantify does not make a risk more important.
wrong_explanations.B: Low likelihood and an existing, tested failover reduce this risk's residual level well below the top candidate.
wrong_explanations.D: Very high impact alone does not make a risk the top priority; its low likelihood lowers the combined rating.

tips: Eliminate: A is moderate on both dimensions, and B is unlikely and already mitigated by a tested failover.
Final two: C beats D because C is high on both likelihood and impact, while D is extreme on impact alone.
Exam cue: rank risks on likelihood and impact together, not on the single scariest dimension.

questions.question: An IS audit manager is designing next year's training. The audit engagements approved for next year cover a cloud migration, AI underwriting models and a legacy mainframe. What is the MOST important consideration?

options.A: Certifications each auditor wants to earn next year
options.B: Competency gaps against the approved audit plan
options.C: Repeating last year's curriculum for consistency

questions.key_concept: Training for an audit team should close gaps between current skills and the competencies the approved audit plan requires.

questions.correct_explanation: The team must collectively hold the skills its planned engagements require, so training should close the gaps between current competencies and what the approved plan demands. Here that includes cloud, AI and mainframe skills. Focusing on emerging technology covers two of the areas, but it neglects the legacy mainframe work in the same plan and is not driven by actual gaps.

wrong_explanations.C: Last year's curriculum fit last year's plan; it may miss the cloud, AI and mainframe skills this year's plan requires.
wrong_explanations.D: Cloud and AI skills are needed, but this focus leaves the planned mainframe audit without trained staff.

tips: Eliminate: A follows individual preference rather than the plan's needs, and C repeats a curriculum built for last year's plan.
Final two: B beats D because training must cover every planned area, including the legacy mainframe, not just new technology.

questions.question: A bank's IS audit function is writing its methodology manual and must state how its auditors treat ITAF guidelines. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Apply them as mandatory, equal to the standards
options.B: Apply them where no standard addresses the topic
options.C: Consider them, and justify any departures from them
options.D: Consult them as reference material when questions arise

questions.key_concept: ITAF standards are mandatory; guidelines are not, but auditors consider them and should be able to justify departures.
questions.pre_read: Two options agree guidelines are not mandatory. Ask what an auditor still owes them.
questions.correct_explanation: ITAF standards are mandatory, while guidelines are not. However, guidelines explain how to apply the standards, so the auditor should consider them, use judgment in applying them and be prepared to justify any departure. Consulting them as reference when questions arise correctly sees that they are not mandatory, but it misses the expectation to consider them on each engagement and explain departures.

wrong_explanations.A: Only the standards are mandatory. Guidelines support applying them, so treating guidelines as binding overstates their authority.
wrong_explanations.B: Guidelines explain how to apply the standards themselves; they are not a fallback reserved for topics the standards leave out.
wrong_explanations.D: Reference-on-demand is fine for ITAF's optional tools and techniques; guidelines sit a tier higher, and for them, non-mandatory does not mean optional.

tips: Eliminate: A makes guidelines mandatory like standards, and B treats them as a gap-filler, though they explain how to apply the standards.
Final two: C beats D because non-mandatory guidelines must still be considered on each engagement, with departures justified, not just consulted when questions arise.
Exam cue: ISACA's ITAF guidelines are not mandatory, but auditors consider them and justify departures; an organization's own guidelines only recommend, so skipping one is no finding.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a daily control that reconciles new clinical-system accounts to the credentialing database and reports accounts lacking a verified credential. Which risk does it MOST directly address?

options.A: Accounts provisioned for staff who are not credentialed
options.B: Departed clinicians keeping access beyond 24 hours
options.C: Shared logins hiding individual accountability
options.D: Outdated or inaccurate records in the central credentialing database

questions.key_concept: A control most directly addresses the risk its design detects or prevents; the reference data it relies on is assumed, not tested.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the control compares, against what, and when. Then match that to the risk.
questions.correct_explanation: The control compares newly created accounts to verified credential records and reports any account without one, so its design targets accounts provisioned for people who lack a verified credential. Outdated database records are a related risk, but the control relies on the database as its reference rather than testing its accuracy, so errors in the database itself would pass unnoticed.

wrong_explanations.B: Revocation after departure concerns existing accounts. A reconciliation of newly created accounts does not detect access that should have been removed.
wrong_explanations.C: Shared logins need individual-account rules and monitoring. A credential reconciliation does not reveal who is using an account.
wrong_explanations.D: The control treats the database as the trusted reference. It does not test whether those records are accurate or current.

tips: Eliminate: B concerns removing existing access, and C concerns shared logins; the control checks neither.
Final two: A beats D because the control uses the database as its benchmark rather than validating it.
Exam cue: map a control to risk by what it compares and when; its reference data is assumed, not tested.

questions.question: An IS auditor must test whether a second-reviewer control operated and estimate the dollar value of mispriced rules. Which sampling approach BEST meets both objectives?

options.A: Attribute sampling for both objectives on one sample
options.B: Variable sampling for the control and attribute sampling for dollar value
options.C: Attribute sampling for the control and variable sampling for dollar value
options.D: Judgmental selection of the highest-value rules

questions.key_concept: Attribute sampling estimates deviation rates for control tests; variable sampling estimates monetary amounts for substantive tests.
questions.pre_read: Classify each objective: is it a yes-or-no question or a how-much question?
questions.correct_explanation: Each objective needs the method built for it. Whether a control operated is a yes-or-no attribute, so attribute sampling estimates the deviation rate. Estimating dollar error needs variable sampling, often monetary-unit sampling. A single attribute sample is efficient and handles the control test, but it yields an error rate, not a projected dollar amount.

wrong_explanations.A: Attribute sampling estimates how often errors occur, not their monetary size, so the dollar objective goes unmet.
wrong_explanations.B: This reverses the methods: variable sampling estimates amounts, not whether a control operated, and attribute sampling yields rates, not dollar values.
wrong_explanations.D: Judgmental selection cannot be projected statistically to the population, so neither objective is supported.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps the two methods, and D cannot be projected to the population.
Final two: C beats A because attribute sampling yields error rates, while the second objective needs a dollar estimate.
Exam cue: yes-or-no control questions take attribute sampling; how-much questions take variable sampling.

questions.question: Business managers dispute an internal IS audit function's right to access their systems. Which document should the head of audit MOST appropriately rely on?

options.A: The approved annual audit plan
options.B: The board-approved IS audit charter
options.C: The engagement letter for the current audit
options.D: The CIO's memo approving this year's audit schedule

questions.key_concept: The audit charter, approved by the board or audit committee, establishes the IS audit function's authority, responsibility and scope.
questions.pre_read: Ask which document grants rights rather than describing work to be done.
questions.correct_explanation: The audit charter, approved by the board or audit committee, formally establishes the audit function's purpose, authority, responsibility and scope, including access to records, systems and people. It is the document that settles disputes about the function's right to act. The annual plan is also approved, but it lists what will be audited, not the authority to demand access.

wrong_explanations.A: The plan schedules engagements and may be approved by the committee, but it does not grant the function authority to access systems.
wrong_explanations.C: An engagement letter confirms one engagement's terms; an internal function draws its authority from the charter rather than from engagement letters.
wrong_explanations.D: Authority to audit cannot come from the management being audited; a CIO memo can be withdrawn and gives no board-level mandate.

tips: Eliminate: C sets terms for one engagement under the charter's authority, and D comes from management, which cannot grant audit its authority.
Final two: B beats A because the charter grants authority and access, while the plan schedules engagements.

questions.question: An IS audit manager is scoping a high-priority content-licensing audit drawn from the risk-based annual plan. What is the MOST important consideration?

options.A: Objectives and boundaries set by identified risks
options.B: Covering every system linked to content licensing
options.C: Matching last year's scope for comparability
options.D: Areas that management's risk register ranks highest

questions.key_concept: Engagement scope comes from defined objectives tied to the risks identified in the risk-based plan, not from maximum coverage.
questions.pre_read: Ask what made this audit high priority. The scope should follow from that, not exceed it.
questions.correct_explanation: Each engagement needs defined objectives, scope and timeframe derived from the risks that placed it in the plan, which keeps work focused and achievable. High priority calls for depth on the risks that matter. Covering every connected system sounds thorough, but it confuses priority with breadth, spreads resources thinly and dilutes attention on the risks that justified the audit.

wrong_explanations.B: Wide coverage would win when building the audit universe, where no system may be missed; within one engagement, scope is drawn around risk, not around connections.
wrong_explanations.C: Last year's scope reflects last year's risks. Copying it ignores changes since then.
wrong_explanations.D: Management's register is useful input, but letting the auditee's ranking set scope compromises independence and may steer the audit away from its risks.

tips: Eliminate: C anchors on last year's risks, and D lets auditees decide what is examined.
Final two: A beats B because risk-based objectives focus effort, while blanket coverage confuses priority with breadth.

questions.question: An IS auditor assesses both inherent risk and control risk as high for a payments system. Which response BEST keeps overall audit risk at an acceptable level?

options.A: Perform more control testing to reduce assessed control risk
options.B: Accept a higher overall audit risk for this engagement
options.C: Lower detection risk by expanding substantive testing
options.D: Reduce sample sizes since controls will be reported as weak

questions.key_concept: Audit risk = inherent risk × control risk × detection risk. The auditor manages audit risk only by adjusting detection risk.
questions.pre_read: Recall the three audit risk components and ask which one the auditor, rather than the auditee, can change.
questions.correct_explanation: In the audit risk model, audit risk is roughly inherent risk times control risk times detection risk. The auditor cannot change inherent or control risk, so when both are high the only lever is lowering detection risk through more extensive substantive procedures. Testing controls more cannot reduce control risk already assessed as high; it only confirms the weakness.

wrong_explanations.A: Control risk belongs to the auditee's environment. More control testing confirms the assessment but does not reduce it, so audit risk stays high.
wrong_explanations.B: The acceptable level of audit risk is set by professional judgment; raising it to fit weak controls defeats the purpose of the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Smaller samples increase detection risk, pushing audit risk higher when the model demands it go lower.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the target instead of meeting it, and D raises detection risk exactly when it must fall.
Final two: C beats A because detection risk is the only component the auditor controls; testing cannot lower control risk.
Exam cue: high inherent or control risk means lower detection risk, which means more or stronger substantive testing.

questions.question: An IS auditor must estimate the dollar value of overbillings in reimbursement claims ranging from $50 to $250,000. Which sampling method is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Attribute sampling of claim approval evidence
options.B: Discovery sampling to find one overbilled claim
options.C: Simple random sampling of individual claims
options.D: Monetary-unit sampling of claim dollar values

questions.key_concept: Monetary-unit sampling selects items with probability proportional to dollar value, suiting substantive tests that estimate dollar misstatement.
questions.pre_read: Note two facts: a dollar estimate is needed and claim values vary widely. Ask which method weights selection by value.
questions.correct_explanation: Monetary-unit sampling treats each dollar as a sampling unit, so selection probability is proportional to size and large claims, where overbillings matter most, are more likely to be tested. It also yields a projected dollar misstatement. Simple random sampling can estimate dollar error too, but it gives a $50 claim the same chance as a $250,000 one.

wrong_explanations.A: Attribute sampling estimates the rate of a control deviation. It does not estimate a dollar amount of misstatement.
wrong_explanations.B: Discovery sampling only shows whether at least one error exists. It cannot estimate the total dollar value of overbilling.
wrong_explanations.C: Random selection is unbiased and statistically valid, but when values vary this widely, selection should follow the dollars that drive misstatement.

tips: Eliminate: A estimates deviation rates, and B only detects whether an error exists; neither projects dollar value.
Final two: D beats C because selection weighted by dollar value concentrates testing on the claims that drive misstatement.
Exam cue: a wide value range plus a dollar misstatement estimate points to monetary-unit sampling.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the quarterly retraining of a real-time fraud-detection model. Which concern about the training data is MOST important?

options.A: Whether the stored training files are encrypted at rest
options.B: Whether retraining occurs often enough to catch new fraud
options.C: Whether training data is representative and accurately labeled
options.D: Whether the training dataset grows larger each quarter

questions.key_concept: Training-data quality, meaning representativeness, freedom from bias and auditable labeling, is the main determinant of an AI model's behavior.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option, if wrong, would make every model decision unreliable regardless of other settings.
questions.correct_explanation: A model learns only what its training data shows, so data that is unrepresentative, biased or wrongly labeled produces systematically wrong fraud scores however often the model is retrained. The auditor should confirm representativeness and a documented, reliable labeling process. Retraining cadence matters, but retraining more often on flawed data simply repeats the flaw faster.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption protects stored data from disclosure, a real control, but it says nothing about whether the data is representative or correctly labeled.
wrong_explanations.B: Stale models do miss new fraud, so retraining cadence is a genuine model control; still, data quality decides model behavior, and inputs are audited before schedules.
wrong_explanations.D: More data is not better data; a growing dataset can still be unrepresentative or mislabeled, so volume does not show quality.

tips: Eliminate: A is a data-security control and D a volume measure; neither shows whether the data teaches the model correct patterns.
Final two: C beats B because data quality determines model behavior; retraining often on flawed data only repeats the flaw.
Exam cue: in AI audits, training data quality, meaning representativeness, bias and labeling, comes before tuning and infrastructure.

questions.question: Applying the fraud triangle, which observation about an accounts payable clerk should an IS auditor treat as the STRONGEST indicator warranting expanded inquiry?

options.A: Sole control of supplier setup, with no vacation in years
options.B: Completion of advanced training on the payables system
options.C: Repeated complaints to coworkers about being underpaid
options.D: Nineteen years of tenure in the same accounts payable role

questions.key_concept: The fraud triangle is pressure, opportunity and rationalization; opportunity indicators such as exclusive control and avoided vacations are most directly observable.
questions.pre_read: Map each observation to a fraud-triangle element, then ask which one the auditor can verify and controls can address.
questions.correct_explanation: Sole control of supplier setup removes segregation of duties, and avoiding vacation prevents the rotation that often exposes concealed fraud. Together they create opportunity, the fraud-triangle element the auditor can observe and test directly. Pay grievances suggest pressure or rationalization and should be noted, but they are common among honest staff and rarely lead to fraud without opportunity.

wrong_explanations.B: Training on the payables system builds competence. It is not a fraud indicator on its own.
wrong_explanations.C: Expressed pay dissatisfaction is a pressure signal shared by many honest employees. Without opportunity, it is weaker grounds for expanded inquiry.
wrong_explanations.D: Long tenure alone is not a fraud indicator. It becomes a concern only when combined with exclusive control or avoided oversight.

tips: Eliminate: D is tenure without any control weakness, and B is normal professional development.
Final two: A beats C because opportunity plus concealment is directly observable, while grievances alone are common among honest staff.
Exam cue: exclusive control combined with avoided vacation or cross-training is a classic opportunity red flag.

questions.question: An audit committee member challenges a conclusion in an IS audit report. Which source should the IS auditor rely on MOST to support the conclusion?

options.A: The annual audit plan approved by the committee
options.B: Management's agreement with the finding at the exit meeting
options.C: The external auditor's agreement with the conclusion

questions.key_concept: Work papers document the evidence, procedures and conclusions of an engagement, providing the support for the audit report.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would let another experienced auditor reach the same conclusion without relying on anyone's word.
questions.correct_explanation: Work papers record the evidence obtained, procedures performed and reasoning behind each conclusion, so they are what substantiates the report when it is challenged. Management's agreement at the exit meeting is persuasive, but agreement is a representation, not evidence; a conclusion must stand on the auditor's documented work even if management later changes its position.

wrong_explanations.A: The audit plan shows which engagements were scheduled, not the evidence for any specific conclusion.
wrong_explanations.B: Management agreement is a representation that can be withdrawn. It supports the relationship, not the evidential basis of the conclusion.
wrong_explanations.C: Another auditor's agreement is an opinion, not evidence; the conclusion must stand on the documented procedures and evidence in the work papers.

tips: Eliminate: C offers another auditor's opinion rather than evidence, and A shows only what was scheduled.
Final two: D beats B because conclusions rest on documented evidence; agreement is a representation that can be withdrawn.

questions.question: An audit manager is introducing two kinds of peer review: one of individual engagement files and one of the practice's overall quality program. What is the MOST important distinction?

options.A: They differ in scope, so both are needed
options.B: Engagement reviews become optional once program reviews occur
options.C: Program reviews give the more reliable view of overall quality
options.D: Engagement reviews are best done by the external assessor

questions.key_concept: Engagement-level peer review assesses one audit's work; program-level review assesses the whole quality program. They complement each other.
questions.pre_read: Ask what question each review answers. If the questions differ, can one replace the other?
questions.correct_explanation: An engagement-level review asks whether one audit's work met standards, while a program-level review asks whether the practice's quality system, methodology and supervision work across engagements. Each answers a different question, so a mature program needs both. Dropping engagement reviews once a program review exists is tempting, but program reviewers sample only a few files.

wrong_explanations.B: Program reviews test the quality system using samples. They cannot replace routine review of individual engagements, where most work-paper problems are caught.
wrong_explanations.C: A program review samples a few files to judge the quality system; it cannot vouch for each engagement, so it answers a different question, not a better one.
wrong_explanations.D: Engagement-level reviews are usually done internally by reviewers not involved in the audit; external assessors typically review the overall program.

tips: Eliminate: C ranks two reviews that answer different questions, and D hands engagement review to the external assessor, who usually reviews the program.
Final two: A beats B because a program review samples only a few files and cannot replace scrutiny of each engagement.

questions.question: An IS auditor's report includes a finding that a senior partner repeatedly accessed deal data beyond assigned scope. Which approach to wording this finding is BEST?

options.A: Let the partner review and reword the finding before issue
options.B: State the facts and evidence in the usual neutral tone
options.C: Move it to a confidential memo for the managing partner
options.D: Use strong wording to stress the seriousness of the conduct

questions.key_concept: Audit findings are reported factually and objectively, with the same rigor regardless of the seniority of those involved.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option keeps the report objective, then check whether it errs toward either softening or dramatizing.
questions.correct_explanation: Audit reports must be objective and evidence-based regardless of who the finding concerns. The partner's conduct is described with the same factual precision as any other finding, neither diluted nor dramatized. Strong wording may seem to protect the organization, but emotive language undermines objectivity and invites challenge; the facts and their impact convey seriousness on their own.

wrong_explanations.A: Inviting the partner to comment seems fair, but the auditor alone sets a finding's wording. The partner may add a response; editing the finding lets the person cited shape it.
wrong_explanations.C: Discretion seems fitting for a sensitive matter, but a reportable finding goes in the report to its usual audience. A side memo removes it from governance oversight.
wrong_explanations.D: An auditor rightly wants the committee to grasp the misconduct, but objectivity runs both ways: a report neither softens nor sharpens for its subject.

tips: Eliminate: A and C, because A lets the person cited reword the finding, and C moves a reportable finding out of the report.
Final two: B beats D because objectivity cuts both ways: no softening and no dramatizing, just facts and impact.
Exam cue: on sensitive findings, choose factual, evidence-based reporting applied equally to everyone.

questions.question: The chief audit executive learns that an exploitable privileged-access flaw may need reporting to a regulator within five days. The flaw was already reported to management, and the committee meets in 45 days. What should the CAE do FIRST?

options.B: Escalate to the audit committee chair now and involve counsel
options.C: Leave the notification decision to the general counsel alone
options.D: Confirm management's remediation plan and escalate if dates slip

questions.key_concept: Critical findings with regulatory exposure warrant prompt escalation to the audit committee chair outside the normal reporting cycle.
questions.pre_read: Compare the deadlines: a five-day notice window against a 45-day meeting gap. Then ask who must know now.
questions.correct_explanation: A critical, exploitable weakness with a possible short regulatory deadline cannot wait for the regular reporting cycle, so the CAE escalates to the audit committee chair between meetings and coordinates with counsel on the notice. Confirming management's remediation plan is sensible follow-up, but it leaves governance uninformed while the exposure and the regulatory clock both run.

wrong_explanations.A: The meeting is 45 days away, far beyond a five-day notice window, and the flaw stays exploitable meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.C: Counsel decides legal questions, but the audit function still owes timely reporting of critical findings to the audit committee.
wrong_explanations.D: An auditor would track the remediation plan in any case, but escalation is triggered by severity and deadlines, not by slipped dates.

tips: Eliminate: A waits 45 days against a five-day window, and C hands the audit function's reporting duty to counsel.
Final two: B beats D because critical findings with regulatory exposure go to governance promptly; management's promise does not replace escalation.
Exam cue: critical severity plus a deadline shorter than the reporting cycle means the CAE escalates to the committee chair between meetings.

questions.subtopic: Control Environment. Independent Evaluation vs Management Monitoring
questions.question: A CFO argues that management's monthly control-monitoring reviews make the IS audit function's independent evaluation duplicative. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Explain that audit also tests whether the monitoring itself works
options.B: Reduce audit testing where monthly monitoring reports no issues
options.C: Invite the monitoring team to co-perform the audit's control testing
options.D: Defer to the regulator's inspections as the independent review

questions.key_concept: Management monitoring and independent evaluation are complementary; audit independently tests controls, including the monitoring itself.
questions.pre_read: Notice who performs the monthly reviews. Ask whether self-review can give the same assurance as an independent evaluation.
questions.correct_explanation: Management monitoring and independent evaluation are complementary parts of internal control. Monitoring is built into operations and catches issues quickly, while independent evaluation gives objective assurance that the controls, including the monitoring itself, work. Reducing testing where monitoring is clean sounds efficient, but it lets management's own unverified results set audit scope.

wrong_explanations.B: Clean monitoring results are management's self-assessment. Using them to cut testing relies on the very process audit should evaluate.
wrong_explanations.C: Management staff testing alongside audit would assess their own monitoring, so the evaluation would no longer be independent.
wrong_explanations.D: Regulators inspect for their own purposes and scope; their work does not replace the organization's independent evaluation.

tips: Eliminate: C has management test its own monitoring within the audit, and D substitutes a regulator's differently scoped work.
Final two: A beats B because monitoring is management's self-review; letting its clean results shrink testing undermines independent assurance.
Exam cue: management monitoring and independent audit evaluation complement each other; neither replaces the other.

questions.question: An audit director is designing the ongoing monitoring element of the quality assurance and improvement program. Which design is BEST?

options.A: An external assessment of the function every five years
options.B: Quarterly self-assessment by each engagement lead against a checklist
options.C: Routine supervision and work-paper review built into every engagement
options.D: An annual deep review of a sample of completed engagements

questions.key_concept: Ongoing QA monitoring is embedded in routine supervision of every engagement; periodic assessments add deeper sampled reviews.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word ongoing. Ask which design operates continuously as part of normal work, not on a schedule.
questions.correct_explanation: Ongoing monitoring is part of the day-to-day management of audit work: routine supervision, work-paper review and standard checklists applied to every engagement. An annual deep review of sampled engagements is valuable, but it is a periodic assessment that complements ongoing monitoring rather than replacing it, and it leaves most work unreviewed between reviews.

wrong_explanations.A: An external assessment is a periodic review by an outside party; ongoing monitoring is built into each engagement between those reviews.
wrong_explanations.B: Leads assessing their own engagements lack objectivity, and a quarterly exercise is periodic rather than built into each engagement as it runs.
wrong_explanations.D: An assessor expects sampled engagement reviews in a mature program, but a yearly sample is periodic, and 'ongoing' means checks inside each engagement.

tips: Eliminate: A is the external assessment, which is periodic, and B has leads assess their own engagements, which lacks objectivity.
Final two: C beats D because ongoing monitoring is built into every engagement; an annual sampled review is a periodic assessment.
Exam cue: ongoing means embedded in daily supervision; periodic means scheduled deeper reviews. Match the word to the design.

questions.question: An IS audit director at a conglomerate operating in 23 countries is establishing the audit universe. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: The IT asset inventory maintained across the 23 countries
options.B: A risk-mapped catalog of auditable entities refreshed periodically
options.C: A static list of divisions set when the function began
options.D: The systems that management has ranked as its highest business risks

questions.key_concept: An audit universe is a complete, risk-mapped catalog of auditable entities at appropriate granularity, refreshed as the organization changes.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the audit universe is for: risk-based planning. Then check completeness, independence and maintenance.
questions.correct_explanation: A well-maintained audit universe catalogs auditable entities such as processes, systems and regulatory obligations at a sensible granularity, maps each to risk, and is refreshed at least annually as the organization changes. Management's high-risk list is a useful input, but it is incomplete and lets the auditee decide what the audit function can see.

wrong_explanations.A: An asset inventory lists technology, not auditable entities mapped to risk; processes and obligations would be missing from the audit universe.
wrong_explanations.C: A static list goes stale as the organization changes, missing new entities, acquisitions and emerging risks.
wrong_explanations.D: Management's ranking shares the catalog's focus on risk, yet it lists only what management chose, and a universe is built for completeness first.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses an asset inventory with an audit universe, and C goes stale as the organization changes.
Final two: B beats D because the audit universe must be complete and independently risk-assessed; management's list is only an input.
Exam cue: the audit universe is complete, risk-mapped and refreshed; beware options that let management define audit coverage.

questions.question: An IS auditor is reviewing the change management process for a point-of-sale system. Which characteristic is MOST important for a well-designed control?

options.A: Developers deploy low-risk changes at their own discretion
options.B: Changes are tested by the developers who wrote them
options.C: Every change is logged as a ticket in one central tool
options.D: Approved changes are migrated by staff outside development

questions.key_concept: Change management controls require authorization, testing, approval and segregation between developing and migrating changes to production.
questions.pre_read: Ask which characteristic prevents an unauthorized or untested change from reaching production, not merely records it.
questions.correct_explanation: A well-designed change control ensures each change is authorized, tested and approved, and moved to production by someone other than the developer, so no single person can introduce an unapproved change. Central ticket logging supports traceability, but a logged change can still be untested or self-deployed, so logging alone does not prevent unauthorized changes.

wrong_explanations.A: Letting developers bypass the process on their own judgment defeats the control and allows unauthorized changes into production.
wrong_explanations.B: Developers testing their own code lose independent challenge; segregating testing and migration from development is what stops unapproved changes.
wrong_explanations.C: Logging provides traceability, but it does not ensure changes are authorized, tested or deployed by someone independent.

tips: Eliminate: A lets developers bypass the control, and B has developers test their own work, which breaks segregation of duties.
Final two: D beats C because authorization, testing and segregation prevent unauthorized changes; logging only records them.
Exam cue: for change management design, look for authorization, testing and segregated migration, not record-keeping alone.

questions.question: In an integrated payroll audit, the IS auditor finds IT general controls over the payroll system ineffective. What is the MOST appropriate effect on the financial testing?

options.A: Increase substantive testing of payroll balances and calculations
options.B: Rely on the automated payroll calculations as planned
options.C: Issue an adverse opinion on payroll without further testing
options.D: Rely more heavily on testing the payroll application controls

questions.key_concept: In an integrated audit, ineffective IT general controls reduce reliance on automated controls and require more substantive testing.
questions.pre_read: Notice which controls failed. Ask what else depends on them in the payroll process.
questions.correct_explanation: Ineffective IT general controls mean automated payroll calculations cannot be assumed to work consistently, so the financial side increases substantive testing of balances and calculations. Leaning on application controls seems a quick fix, but application controls depend on the general controls beneath them, so their reliability is undermined too.

wrong_explanations.B: Automated calculations cannot be relied on when the general controls that protect them are ineffective.
wrong_explanations.C: An opinion needs evidence; weak IT controls call for more testing before concluding.
wrong_explanations.D: As with the key, heavier application testing seeks assurance elsewhere; once general controls fail, though, assurance must come from the data itself.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on automated calculations whose general controls failed, and C concludes before gathering evidence.
Final two: A beats D because application controls rest on general controls; when those fail, substantive testing fills the gap.
Exam cue: weak IT general controls reduce reliance on automated controls and increase substantive testing.

questions.question: An IS auditor will sample user-access changes from a ticketing system extract. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Calculate sample size from confidence level and expected error
options.B: Accept the extract since it came directly from the system
options.C: Select tickets from the teams that are easiest to reach
options.D: Confirm the extract is complete and fits the audit objective

questions.key_concept: A sample conclusion is valid only for the population sampled, so the auditor first defines the population against the objective and verifies its completeness.
questions.pre_read: A perfect sample of the wrong or incomplete population still gives the wrong answer. Decide what comes before any sizing.
questions.correct_explanation: Population definition comes first: the auditor confirms the extract contains every item the conclusion will cover and nothing outside the objective, for example by reconciling ticket counts to the source system. Sample sizing matters, but it is calculated for a defined population; sizing an incomplete extract only produces a precise answer about the wrong set of items.

wrong_explanations.A: Sizing from confidence and expected error is the standard method, though sampling runs in a fixed order: population, method, size, then items.
wrong_explanations.B: System-generated extracts can still be filtered or incomplete. The auditor independently verifies completeness before relying on them.
wrong_explanations.C: Convenience selection introduces bias and does not support projecting results to the population.

tips: Eliminate: B skips completeness verification of a system extract, and C is a biased convenience selection.
Final two: D beats A because sizing is meaningless until the population is confirmed complete and aligned with the objective.
Exam cue: in sampling sequences, define and verify the population before choosing method, size or items.

questions.subtopic: Sampling. Precision Setting (Acceptable Risk Levels and Tolerable Error)
questions.question: An IS auditor assesses inherent and control risk as high for shipping-fee transactions. Which precision setting for the substantive sample is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Lower the risk of incorrect acceptance and base tolerable error on materiality
options.B: Lower the risk of incorrect acceptance and set tolerable error near zero
options.C: Raise the risk of incorrect acceptance, as controls are unreliable
options.D: Reuse last year's parameters for consistency across periods

questions.key_concept: High inherent and control risk call for a low acceptable risk of incorrect acceptance, while tolerable error is set from materiality.
questions.pre_read: There are two parameters here. Decide what drives each one: the assessed risk, or the size of error that would matter.
questions.correct_explanation: When inherent and control risk are high, detection risk must be low, so the auditor lowers the acceptable risk of incorrect acceptance and enlarges the sample. Tolerable error is a separate judgment derived from materiality for the assertion. Setting it near zero sounds conservative, but it is not anchored to what would matter to users and drives sample sizes beyond any practical, risk-based need.

wrong_explanations.B: Like the materiality-based setting, it lowers the risk of incorrect acceptance as high risk demands, but tolerable error always derives from materiality.
wrong_explanations.C: High control risk requires more substantive assurance, so the risk of incorrect acceptance should fall, not rise.
wrong_explanations.D: Precision parameters follow the current risk assessment; reusing prior values ignores changes in risk and population.

tips: Eliminate: C moves the risk of incorrect acceptance the wrong way, and D reuses prior parameters instead of the current risk assessment.
Final two: A beats B because tolerable error is a materiality judgment; near zero is not risk-based and makes sampling impractical.
Exam cue: higher assessed risk means lower acceptable sampling risk and bigger samples; tolerable error comes from materiality.

questions.subtopic: SOC Report Types. Type 1 vs Type 2 Reliance
questions.question: An IS auditor must conclude on a SaaS provider's controls across the past year, but only a SOC 2 Type 1 report is available. What is the BEST course of action?

options.A: Obtain other evidence that the controls operated throughout the year
options.B: Accept management's written assertion that the controls operated year-round
options.C: Rely on the Type 1 report once its scope matches the services
options.D: Report the provider's controls as ineffective for the whole year

questions.key_concept: A SOC 2 Type 1 report covers control design at a point in time; a Type 2 adds operating effectiveness over a period.
questions.pre_read: Notice the conclusion covers a whole year. Ask whether a point-in-time report can show controls operated over that period.
questions.correct_explanation: A Type 1 report describes control design at a single date, so it cannot show the controls operated effectively across the year. The auditor needs further evidence of operation, such as a Type 2 report or the auditor's own tests. Confirming the Type 1 scope is useful, but a correctly scoped point-in-time report still says nothing about operation over the period.

wrong_explanations.B: A management assertion is not independent evidence. The provider's own claim cannot replace tested evidence of operating effectiveness.
wrong_explanations.C: Scope matters, but even a well-scoped Type 1 shows design at one date only, not operation across the period.
wrong_explanations.D: Missing period evidence is not proof of failure. Concluding the controls are ineffective without testing them is unsupported.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the provider's own claim, and D concludes failure without any evidence of it.
Final two: A beats C because a Type 1 shows design at one date; correct scope cannot turn it into period evidence.
Exam cue: a conclusion about a period needs Type 2 or equivalent evidence; Type 1 supports only design at a date.

questions.question: An IS audit manager's team has strong general IT skills but no industrial control system experience for an upcoming ICS security audit. What should the manager do FIRST?

options.A: Start fieldwork and let the team learn ICS on the job
options.B: Reassign the audit to another internal team with prior ICS experience
options.C: Identify the specific skill gaps and plan targeted expert support
options.D: Remove the ICS audit from the annual audit plan

questions.key_concept: Before an engagement starts, the manager diagnoses specific competency gaps and closes them through experts, training or co-sourcing.
questions.pre_read: The team is strong but lacks one specialty. Ask what must be understood before choosing any fix.
questions.correct_explanation: The manager first pins down which ICS knowledge is missing, such as industrial protocols or safety systems, then closes the gap with an expert, targeted training or co-sourcing. Reassigning to an experienced team may work, but it skips the diagnosis, assumes such a team is available, and may sacrifice the existing team's strong IT knowledge that the audit still needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Learning on the job means fieldwork starts without the proficiency the engagement requires, risking missed ICS-specific issues.
wrong_explanations.B: A team with ICS experience does bring the missing proficiency, but a competency gap is sized before it is filled.
wrong_explanations.D: A skills gap does not remove the risk. Dropping a planned audit leaves an important area without coverage.

tips: Eliminate: A starts without proficiency, and D removes coverage of a risk area instead of fixing the gap.
Final two: C beats B because diagnosing the gap comes first and allows a targeted fix that keeps useful existing skills.
Exam cue: for competency gaps, diagnose first, then supplement with experts or training before fieldwork.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that no member of a bank's audit committee has technology risk experience, though cyber risk tops the risk register. What should the auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Appoint the CIO to the audit committee as a voting member
options.B: Add an independent director with technology expertise to the committee
options.C: Delegate IT risk oversight to the management IT steering committee
options.D: Give committee members an annual briefing on technology risk

questions.key_concept: An audit committee needs members able to challenge management on its top risks; add independent expertise, never management members, to close a skills gap.
questions.pre_read: Notice which risk tops the register and who on the committee can judge it. Ask which fix keeps the committee independent.
questions.correct_explanation: The audit committee must be able to question management on the bank's biggest risk, and today no member can. Adding an independent director with technology expertise gives the committee that competence without compromising its independence. An annual briefing is the tempting option: it raises awareness, but one session does not give members the depth to challenge management's cyber decisions throughout the year.

wrong_explanations.A: The CIO is management. As a voting member, the CIO would help oversee their own decisions, which undermines the committee's independence.
wrong_explanations.C: The steering committee is a management body. Board oversight of the top risk cannot be handed to the managers being overseen.
wrong_explanations.D: Technology briefings are fine for keeping a capable committee current, but a body lacking expertise usually closes the gap through its membership.

tips: Eliminate: A puts management on the committee that oversees it, and C hands board oversight to a management body.
Final two: B beats D because a member with real expertise can challenge management all year; an annual briefing only builds awareness.
Exam cue: an oversight body needs both competence and independence; close a skills gap without putting management on it.

questions.question: After an IS audit report is issued, a research committee asks that findings on research access be removed to protect its reputation. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Issue a separate version of the report for the committee
options.B: Remove the findings, since research access carries lower risk
options.C: Add a note that research access was outside the audit's main focus
options.D: Retain the findings and review the evidence with the committee

questions.key_concept: Reported findings change only on new evidence; stakeholder disagreement is addressed by discussing the factual basis.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would legitimately change a finding. Stakeholder preference is not on that list.
questions.correct_explanation: Audit findings rest on evidence, not on how stakeholders feel about them. The auditor keeps the findings and engages the committee on facts, correcting only if evidence shows an error. Adding a note that downplays research access seems like a harmless compromise, but it misrepresents the audit's scope and still bends the report to stakeholder pressure.

wrong_explanations.A: Different versions for different readers produce inconsistent conclusions and undermine the report's objectivity.
wrong_explanations.B: The committee's preference is not evidence of lower risk; removing supported findings sacrifices objectivity.
wrong_explanations.C: Scope notes are legitimate when they state what was actually covered, but report content moves only with evidence, never with a reader's comfort.

tips: Eliminate: A creates inconsistent versions of the report, and B removes findings without evidence.
Final two: D beats C because a scope note that softens findings still yields to pressure; only evidence should change a report.
Exam cue: when stakeholders object to findings, discuss the facts but change the report only if the evidence changes.

questions.question: The audit committee chair proposes amending the audit charter so IS audit advises operations on control design before implementation. What is the audit director's BEST response?

options.A: Raise the self-review threat and propose recusal safeguards
options.B: Accept the amendment, as early advice improves control design
options.C: Route advisory requests to a single junior auditor
options.D: Reject it, as an approved charter should not be amended

questions.key_concept: Advisory work on controls the function later audits creates a self-review threat that needs disclosure and recusal safeguards.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens when audit later tests the controls it helped design.
questions.correct_explanation: Advising on control design and later auditing the same controls creates a self-review threat. The director should explain that threat and offer a workable model, such as disclosed advisory work with recusal of those involved from later audits. Accepting the amendment unchanged captures real value from early input, but leaves the independence threat unmanaged.

wrong_explanations.B: Early advice does add value, but accepting without safeguards leaves the function auditing its own recommendations.
wrong_explanations.C: Seniority does not remove a self-review threat; a junior auditor advising on controls the function later audits faces the same conflict.
wrong_explanations.D: Charters can and should be updated; the issue is the independence safeguards, not whether amendments are allowed.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes seniority affects independence, and D treats the charter as unchangeable.
Final two: A beats B because advisory work is acceptable only with safeguards; accepting unchanged leaves auditors reviewing their own advice.
Exam cue: when audit is offered an advisory role, name the independence threat and propose safeguards; decline only roles no safeguard can fix, such as advising on work under audit.

questions.question: Mid-fieldwork, an IS auditor finds that operations gave inaccurate planning information, which undermines the risk assessment. The audit committee meets tomorrow to decide the engagement's future. What should the audit director do FIRST?

options.A: Continue fieldwork as planned and note the issue in the report
options.B: Pause work and brief the audit committee on options
options.C: Have operations correct the information, then resume fieldwork
options.D: Revise the risk assessment and expand scope immediately

questions.key_concept: When material new facts undermine an engagement, pause, document and let the audit committee decide how to proceed.
questions.pre_read: Notice the risk assessment is now unreliable and the committee is already engaged. Ask who should decide the next step.
questions.correct_explanation: When the basis of the engagement is undermined, the director should pause, document why, and give the audit committee options such as resuming, expanding scope or stopping, so the decision is informed and authorized. Revising the plan is a natural audit reaction, but expanding scope alone preempts a committee that meets tomorrow to decide the engagement's future.

wrong_explanations.A: The plan rests on a risk assessment now known to be unreliable; continuing produces conclusions on a flawed basis.
wrong_explanations.C: Correcting the data does not settle whether the engagement should continue as planned; the committee meeting tomorrow must decide with full information.
wrong_explanations.D: An auditor would expect a revised risk assessment before fieldwork resumes, but with the committee meeting tomorrow, material changes are its call.

tips: Eliminate: A carries on with a flawed plan, and C lets the auditee repair the basis and resumes without the committee that must decide.
Final two: B beats D because material changes need the committee's decision; expanding scope alone preempts its governance role.
Exam cue: audit revises its own program or plan when risks change; when the engagement's basis collapses and governance is about to decide its future, pause and give them options.
